dialogues.title: Dialogue 1
dialogues.setting: Miss Wong and Miss Cheung are shopping in a fashion store

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 今日係礼拜一，唔係礼拜日，点解呢间铺头咁多人呢？
lines.jp: gam1 jat6 hai6 lai5 baai3 jat1, m4 hai6 lai5 baai3 jat6, dim2 gaai2 ni1 gaan1 pou3 tau2 gam3 do1 jan4 ne1?
lines.en: Today is Monday, not Sunday, how come this store is so crowded?

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 呢间铺头大减价吖嘛。我地入去睇吓好吗？
lines.jp: ni1 gaan1 pou3 tau2 daai6 gaam2 gaa3 aa1 maa3. ngo5 dei6 jap6 heoi3 tai2 haa5 hou2 maa1?
lines.en: This store is having a big sale. Let's go inside and check it out, ok?

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 好呀，哇！你睇，嗰件衫裙真係好平啵！
lines.jp: hou2 aa3, waa3! nei5 tai2, go2 gin6 saam1 kwan4 zan1 hai6 hou2 peng4 bo3!
lines.en: Sure. Wow! Look, that dress is really cheap!

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 係啵。质地又好；款式又新；颜色又靓；真係好勒。
lines.jp: hai6 bo3. zat1 dei2 jau6 hou2; fun2 sik1 jau6 san1; ngaan4 sik1 jau6 leng3; zan1 hai6 hou2 laak3.
lines.en: You are right! The quality is good, the style is new, the color is pretty, it's really good

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 咁，我就买呢件喇。
lines.jp: gam2, ngo5 zau6 maai5 ni1 gin6 laa1.
lines.en: Then, I'll buy this one

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 我都想买嗰件红色嘅。
lines.jp: ngo5 dou1 soeng2 maai5 go2 gin6 hung4 sik1 ge3.
lines.en: I also want to buy that red one

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 咦，呢处有少少烂咗啵。
lines.jp: ji2, ni1 cyu3 jau5 siu2 siu2 laan6 zo2 bo3.
lines.en: What's this? There's a small tear here

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 係咩？哦！係啵！我呢件都有少少烂咗。等我睇下其他嘅有冇烂呢。
lines.jp: hai6 me1? ngo4! hai6 bo3! ngo5 ni1 gin6 dou1 jau5 siu2 siu2 laan6 zo2. dang2 ngo5 tai2 haa5 kei4 taa1 ge3 jau5 mou5 laan6 ne1.
lines.en: Really? Oh! right! Mine also has a small tear. Let me see if there are others that have tears

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 唔使睇啦，件件都有少少烂嘅，因为佢地都係次货，所以咁平。
lines.jp: m4 sai2 tai2 laa1, gin6 gin6 dou1 jau5 siu2 siu2 laan6 ge3, jan1 wai4 keoi5 dei6 dou1 hai6 ci3 fo3, so2 ji5 gam3 peng4.
lines.en: No need to look, every one has a small tear. Because they are all seconds, therefore they are so cheap

lines.jp: ni1 di1 haa1 gam3 sai3, baat3 sap6 ng5 man1 jat1 gan1 taai3 gwai3 laak3. cat1 sap6 man1 jat1 gan1 dak1 m4 dak1 aa3?

lines.speaker: Seller

lines.speaker: Cheung

grammar.title: The week
grammar.summary: lai5 baai3 (or sing1 kei4) means week and is classified with go3. Monday to Saturday are numbered 1-6; Sunday uses jat6 'sun'.
grammar.body:
lai5 baai3 means week: it is classified with go3, so one week is jat1 go3 lai5 baai3, two weeks is loeng5 go3 lai5 baai3 and so on.
The days of the week are simply numbered 1-6 from Monday to Saturday.
Sunday is not numbered, instead the word for sun jat6 is used, so lai5 baai3 jat6 is Sunday. Go very carefully with your tones or you will mix up Sunday (lai5 baai3 jat6) and Monday (lai5 baai3 jat1).
Some people say sing1 kei4 instead of lai5 baai3 and you may do so too if you wish. Simply substitute sing1 kei4 for lai5 baai3 in any of the words in the above list.

grammar.title: Ne1 again
grammar.summary: ne1 also ends rhetorical questions, when no answer is expected or you are wondering to yourself.
grammar.body: We have met ne1? as a final particle which asks a follow-up question. It is also used after rhetorical questions, that is when you do not expect an answer or perhaps when you are wondering to yourself.

examples.jp: go2 go3 jan4 hai6 bin1 go3 ne1?
examples.en: I wonder who that can be?

grammar.title: The verbs heoi3 'go' and lai4 'come' (i): as main verbs
grammar.summary: heoi3 and lai4 are used by themselves as main verbs and can be followed directly by a destination.
grammar.body:
(i) used by themselves as main verbs.
Both can be followed directly by a place name or other expression of the destination.

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 jat1 cai4 heoi3 laa1
keoi5 ting1 jat6 m4 lai4 laa3
ngo5 jat1 jyut6 heoi3 mei5 gwok3
examples.en: I'm going to America in January

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 ji4 gaa1 heoi3 fo2 ce1 zaam6
examples.en: We're going to the railway station now

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 m4 lai4 jing1 gwok3
nei5 gei2 si4 lai4 ngo5 nguk1 kei5 aa3?
examples.en: When are you coming to my place?

grammar.title: The verbs heoi3 'go' and lai4 'come' (ii): with directional verbs
grammar.summary: Directional verbs (jap6, ceot1, soeng5, lok6, gwo3, faan1) combine with heoi3/lai4 and are used like simple verbs.
grammar.body:
(ii) used together with directional verbs.
These combinations are used in the same way as the simple verbs.

examples.jp: ngo5 soeng5 heoi3 bak1 ging1 hoi1 wui2
examples.en: I'm going up to Beijing for a meeting
examples.lit: I ascend go Beijing hold meeting

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 lok6 heoi3 sik6 faan6 laa1
examples.lit: We descend go eat rice

examples.jp: nei5 gei2 si4 gwo3 lai4 taam3 ngo5 aa3?
examples.en: When are you coming over to visit me?
examples.lit: You when over come visit me

grammar.title: The verbs heoi3 'go' and lai4 'come' (iii): manner verbs and objects
grammar.summary: A manner verb can precede the directional verb (manner-direction-come/go); with a transitive verb, the directional verb and heoi3/lai4 follow the object.
grammar.body:
A third verb may be added before the directional verb to express the manner of movement, resulting in a sequence of three verbs: (manner-direction-come/go).
When used with a transitive verb, the directional verb and heoi3/lai4 follow the object.

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 soeng2 daai3 di1 san1 tung4 si6 jap6 lai4
examples.en: We'd like to bring in some new colleagues
examples.lit: We wish to bring some new colleagues in come

examples.jp: ngo5 ling1 di1 hang4 lei5 soeng5 lai4 sin1
examples.en: I'll bring the luggage up first
examples.lit: I carry the luggage up come first

examples.jp: m4 goi1 nei5 dai6 di1 sung3 gwo3 lai4
examples.en: Could you pass the dishes over, please
examples.lit: Please you pass the food over come

grammar.title: The verbs heoi3 'go' and lai4 'come' (iv): aspect markers and serial verbs
grammar.summary: Aspect markers zo2 and gan2 go after the first verb of the sequence; four-verb patterns with both lai4 and heoi3 mean 'back and forth'.
grammar.body:
Aspect marker like zo2 '-ed' and gan2 '-ing' appear after the first verb of the sequence.
These sequences of verbs are known as serial verb constructions. One such pattern, using both lai4 and heoi3, uses four verbs in a row.

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 ceot1 zo2 heoi3 hou2 noi6 laa3
examples.en: They've been out for a long time

examples.jp: lou5 baan2 faan1 gan2 lai4 ge3 laa3
examples.en: The boss is on his way (lit. coming) back

examples.jp: zek3 zoek3 zai2 fei1 zo2 jap6 lai4 cyu4 fong2
examples.en: The bird has flown into the kitchen

examples.jp: di1 seoi2 lau6 gan2 lok6 lai4 haa6 min6

grammar.title: The verbs heoi3 'go' and lai4 'come' (v): directional verbs with place objects
grammar.summary: Directional verbs are also verbs in their own right, taking a place expression as object; this gives several set phrases.
grammar.body: Directional verbs are also used as verbs in their own right, with a place expression as their object. This pattern includes a number of useful set phrases.

examples.en: Get on/off a car, bus, etc.

grammar.title: Another verb ending: -haa5
grammar.summary: -haa5 after a verb gives the idea of doing something for a bit.
grammar.body: In unit 4 we met the verb ending -zo2, -gan2. Another one is -haa5, which gives the idea of doing something for a bit.

examples.en: Have a glance at (look a bit)
Wait for a moment (wait a bit)
Sit for a while (sit a bit)

grammar.title: jau6 … jau6 …: both…and…
grammar.summary: jau6 'furthermore' is an adverb, so it comes in front of each verb even when repeated to mean both…and…
grammar.body: jau6 basically means furthermore and it is an adverb. It has to obey the rule for such adverbs and comes in front of verbs, even when it is being repeated to give the meaning both…and… In the dialogue, we see that it does obey (the three verbs are hou2 to be good, san1 to be new, and leng3 to be pretty).

examples.jp: Wong4 sin1 saang1 jau6 heoi3, Wong4 taai3 taai2 jau6 heoi3
examples.en: Both Mr. and Mrs. Wong are going

grammar.title: Colors
grammar.summary: hung4 'red' is normally used as hung4 sik1 'red-colored'; ge3 links it to a noun.
grammar.body: hung4 means red, but it is most easily used in combination with sik1 color as hung4 sik1 red-colored. ge3 is added to link hung4 sik1 with a noun.

examples.jp: keoi5 ge3 ce1 hai6 mat1 je5 ngaan4 sik1 gaa3?

grammar.title: Here and there
grammar.summary: here = ni1 cyu3 / ni1 dou6 (this place); there = go2 cyu3 / go2 dou6 (that place).
grammar.body: In Unit 3 we met bin1 cyu3 and bin1 dou6 where bin1 means which? And cyu3 and dou6 both mean place, so which place? And where? Logically enough, here and there made from this place and that place.

grammar.title: Final particle me1
grammar.summary: me1 turns a question into an expression of great surprise or disbelief; the answer is almost always hai6 or m4 hai6.
grammar.body:
If you want to express great incredulity in a question in English (You can speak 57 languages fluently?!) you raise your voice almost to a squeak at the end of the question; but of course it is less easy to do that in Cantonese because of the need to observe tone. me1 does the job for you.
It indicates great surprise, astonishment, near disbelief, surely that's not the case, is it? Do you mean to say that…? The answer given is almost always hai6 or m4 hai6 (it is the case or it is not the case).

grammar.title: dang2 again
grammar.summary: dang2 ngo5 means wait for me (to) and, at the start of a sentence, let me…
grammar.body:
dang2 means to wait, dang2 ngo5 means wait for me or wait for me to.
From wait for me to eat to let me eat is not a big jump and you will find that Cantonese often uses dang2 ngo5 where English would say let me… Generally if dang2 ngo5 comes at the beginning of a sentence it is likely to be used in the sense of let me…; and if it comes embedded in a sentence then it is likely to mean wait for.

examples.jp: m4 hou2 dang2 ngo5 sik6 faan6
examples.en: Don't wait for me to eat

grammar.title: Double classifiers
grammar.summary: Doubling a classifier and adding dou1 before the verb means every one of, each one of.
grammar.body: Doubling-up classifiers and adding dou1 all before the verb is a useful way of conveying the idea every one of, each one of.

examples.jp: gaan1 gaan1 nguk1 dou1 hou2 leng3
zi1 zi1 mei5 gwok3 bat1 dou1 gwai3
gin6 gin6 saam1 kwan4 dou1 m4 peng4

grammar.title: So much each
grammar.summary: Prices and rates use the formula: amount + man1 + jat1 + classifier (e.g. loeng5 man1 jat1 gan1, $2 a catty).
grammar.body:
Note the simple formula for giving prices.
The same kind of formula can be used with other terms.

examples.jp: A: gei2 do1 cin2 jat1 gan1 aa3?
jat1 go3 jan4 jat1 zi1 bat1

grammar.title: How about it? Again
grammar.summary: dak1 m4 dak1 aa3? asks for someone's agreement after a statement: will that do? is that OK by you?
grammar.body: In Unit 2 we met hou2 m4 hou2 aa3? as a way of asking someone's opinion after making a statement. dak1 m4 dak1 aa3? is perhaps even more commonly used for the same purpose, meaning will that do?, is that OK by you? Are you happy with that?

examples.en: How about it? (asking someone's opinion after a statement)
Will that do? Is that OK by you? Are you happy with that?

grammar.title: Thank you
grammar.summary: m4 goi1 is for everyday minor politeness; do1 ze6 is for heartfelt thanks and is always used when receiving money. The polite response is m4 sai2.
grammar.body:
You have now met two words for thank you: m4 goi1 and do1 ze6. They are used in different ways and it is important to try to sort them out.
m4 goi1 is used for everyday minor politeness, such as thanking someone for holding a door open for you, for passing you the soy sauce, or for doing the washing-up.
do1 ze6 is used for more heartfelt thanks, for example in gratitude to someone for a present received, for saving your life or for finding you a job. It is always used when receiving money.
So, when you take the goods from a shopkeeper, you may or may not say m4 goi1 (depending how polite you feel like being), but he will certainly say do1 ze6 when he takes your money. The polite response to someone who thanks you is m4 sai2.

examples.en: Thank you (heartfelt; always when receiving money)
There's no need to (reply to m4 goi1)
There's no need to (reply to do1 ze6)

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner with dak1
grammar.summary: Manner adverbs follow the pattern verb - dak1 - adjective; if the verb has an object, the verb is repeated so dak1 follows it directly.
grammar.body:
Several types of adverb phrase can be used to modify a verb or verb phrase.
With dak1 (word order: verb - dak1 - adjective).
When the verb is followed by an object, the verb is repeated so that dak1 immediately follows the verb.

examples.jp: gaa3 ce1 haang4 dak1 hou2 maan6
examples.lit: The car travel manner very slow

examples.jp: di1 haak3 jan4 sik6 dak1 gei2 hoi1 sam1
examples.en: The guests are eating quite happily
examples.lit: The guests eat manner quite happy

examples.jp: go3 gong2 si1 gong2 dak1 taai3 faai3
examples.lit: The lecturer speak manner too fast

examples.jp: ngo5 coeng3 go1 coeng3 dak1 hou2 caa1
examples.lit: I sing songs sing manner very bad

examples.jp: keoi5 waak3 waa2 waak3 dak1 gei2 leng3
examples.lit: She paints pictures paints manner quite nice

examples.jp: nei5 gong2 je5 gong2 dak1 taai3 daai6 seng1
examples.lit: You speak things speak manner too big voice

grammar.title: Adverb phrases with gam2
grammar.summary: Adjective + gam2 'thus' forms an adverbial phrase placed before the verb; gam2 joeng2 means 'in this way'.
grammar.body:
An adjective together with gam2 'thus' forms an adverbial phrase which comes before the verb.
The use of gam2 by itself vs. gam2 joeng2 to mean 'in this way'.

examples.jp: di1 gun1 zung3 hou2 daai6 seng1 gam2 paak3 sau2
examples.lit: The audience very big voice thus clap hands

examples.jp: go3 jau4 haak3 hou2 jau5 lai5 maau6 gam2 man6 ngo5
examples.en: The tourist asked me very politely
examples.lit: The tourist very politely thus asked me

examples.jp: go3 si1 gei1 hou2 daai6 lik6 gam2 saan1 mun4
examples.en: The driver closed the door hard
examples.lit: The driver very big-force thus closed door

examples.en: I wouldn't put it like that

examples.jp: keoi5 m4 jing1 goi1 gam2 joeng2 saai1 cin2
examples.en: He shouldn't waste money in this way

grammar.title: Reduplicated adverbs
grammar.summary: Some manner adverbs repeat an adjective and add -dei2 (or no suffix); the repeated syllable may change to a high rising tone; two-syllable adjectives repeat each syllable separately.
grammar.body:
A limited number of adverbs of manner are formed by repeating an adjective and adding the suffix -dei2.
These are placed before the verb they modify.
A few such forms are also used without -dei2.
The repeated adverb may take on a changed tone (with a low tone becoming a high rising tone).
In adjectives with two syllables, each syllable is repeated separately.

examples.jp: nei5 jiu3 gwaai1 gwaai1 dei2 zou6 gung1 fo3
examples.en: You have to obediently do your homework
examples.lit: You need obediently do homework

examples.jp: jau5 jan4 heng1 heng1 dei2 paak3 mun4
examples.en: Someone knocks lightly on the door
examples.lit: Have person lightly knock door

examples.jp: hoi1 hoi1 sam1 sam1 zou6 je5

grammar.title: Position of adverbs of manner
grammar.summary: All these adverb forms come before the verb; reduplicated adverbs (especially multi-syllable ones) can combine with gam2.
grammar.body:
All these forms of adverb come before the verb they modify.
Reduplicated adverbs, especially those of more than one syllable, can combine with gam2 as described in above.

examples.jp: nei5 zing6 zing2 dei2 jap6 heoi3 laa1
keoi5 tau1 tau1 dei2 zau2 zo2
keoi5 gaan2 gaan2 daan1 daan1 gam2 hing3 zuk1 saang1 jat6
examples.en: She celebrated her birthday in a simple way

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 hing1 hing1 sung1 sung1 gaan2 gaan2 daan1 daan1 gam2 dou6 gaa3
examples.en: We spend our holiday in a laid-back, simple style

examples.jp: keoi5 so4 so2 dei6 gam2 siu3
examples.en: He smiles in a foolish way

examples.jp: nei5 syu1 syu1 fuk6 fuk6 gam2 fan3 hai2 dou6
keoi5 dei6 hai2 dou6 hing1 hing1 sung1 sung1 gam2 teng1 go1
examples.en: They're listening to songs in a relaxed manner

grammar.title: Adverbs of time
grammar.summary: Cantonese verbs do not show tense, so time adverbs (now, just now, before, tomorrow…) specify when; they come before the verb or before the subject.
grammar.body:
Adverbs of time: since verbs do not indicate tense in Cantonese, adverbs are especially important in specifying when events take place.
In English the tense of the verb indicates when things take place and the adverb can easily be omitted, but in Cantonese only the adverb indicates the time.
Present: ji4 gaa1 now, gam1 jat6 today. Recent past: tau4 sin1 just now, ngaam1 ngaam1 just. Past: zi1 cin4 before, bun2 loi4 originally, soeng6 ci3 last time, go2 zan6 si4 then, kam4 jat6 yesterday, cin4 jat6 the day before yesterday. Future: zik1 haak1 right away / immediately, dai6 ji6 si4 / dai6 si4 in the future, haa6 ci3 next time, dou3 si4 when the time comes, ting1 jat6 tomorrow, hau6 jat6 the day after tomorrow.
Adverbs of time may come before the verb.
Adverbs of time may come before the subject.

grammar.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammar.summary: Frequency adverbs (sing4 jat6 always, jat1 ci3 once…) and mui5 'each' phrases; one-syllable time words reduplicate (jat6 jat6) and take no classifier; 'once a year' phrases are often split around the verb.
grammar.body:
Useful adverbs to describe the frequency of an action include: sing4 jat6 always, do1 sou3 mostly, jau5 (zan6) si4 sometimes, jat1 si4 si4 / jat1 si2 si4 occasionally, ping4 si4 normally, jat1 ci3 once, loeng5 ci3 twice, saam1 ci3 three times, gei2 ci3 several times, ging1 soeng4 usually.
mui5 'each' can be used to form adverbial phrases.
Several common time expressions of one syllable do not take a classifier, and can form reduplicated adverbs: mui5 ci3 or ci3 ci3 (not *mui5 go3 ci3), mui5 jat6 or jat6 jat6 (not *mui5 go3 jat6), mui5 nin4 or nin4 nin4 (not *mui5 go3 nin4), mui5 ziu1 or ziu1 ziu1 (not *mui5 go3 ziu1), mui5 maan5 or maan5 maan5 (not *mui5 go3 maan5).
They generally come before the verb.
The order in phrases such as the following describing the frequency of the action: jat1 nin4 jat1 ci3 (lit. one year one time).
Such phrases are often split up with the more general term coming before the verb and the more specific frequency expression after.
Adverbs of frequency may come after the verb and object.

examples.jp: jat1 si4 si4 / jat1 si2 si4
keoi5 mui5 ziu1 luk6 dim2 hei2 san1 ge3
examples.en: He gets up at six every morning
examples.lit: He each morning six o'clock gets up

examples.en: She washes her hair every day
examples.lit: She daily washes hair
One year one time
Each month one time

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 jat1 nin4 heoi3 jat1 ci3 dou6 gaa3
examples.en: We go on holiday once a year
examples.lit: We one year go one time spend holiday

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 nin4 nin4 faan1 heoi3 jat1 ci3
examples.en: We go back once a year
examples.lit: We each year return go one time

examples.jp: ngo5 heoi3 gwo3 daai6 luk6 jat1 ci3
examples.en: I've been to mainland China once

examples.jp: ngo5 gin3 gwo3 ji1 sang1 saam1 ci3
examples.en: I've seen the doctor three times

grammar.title: Adverbs of frequency and duration: position
grammar.summary: Frequency and duration expressions go either between the verb and its object, or after verb + object with the transitive verb repeated.
grammar.body:
Adverbs of both frequency and duration can be used in the following ways:
(i) Between the verb and the object.
(ii) After the verb and object, with repetition of the transitive verb.

examples.en: I've been to the mainland once

notes.title: Let me pay!
notes.body:
In restaurants you will often hear Chinese customers vying with each other to pay the bill. The winner gaining in "face" what he/she loses in pocket. The standard wording used is dang2 ngo5 bei2 Let me pay! (lit: let me give!)
You too can play that game, but be sure you have the money about you in case you should be (un)lucky enough to win!
